beats.script_body: Touring Harlem takes imagination, because much of what made it unique during the fabled Jazz Era — the Harlem Renaissance — crumbled beneath the wrecking ball decades ago. The wide avenues, rows of brownstones, and elegant apartment buildings you see now are an accident of history: the physical face of an area that housed a people but wasn't necessarily 'of' that people. Despite all this, Harlem remains the African-American capital of the United States, sometimes called the 'capital for Africans throughout the world.' As architect Zevilla Jackson Preston writes in HarlemWorld, 'Ultimately it is the energy on the street, the beat on the street — all of the beautiful Black people on the streets — that make the experience unique.'
key_claims: Much of Jazz-Era Harlem was demolished decades ago
Harlem remains the African-American capital of the US
Zevilla Jackson Preston quote from HarlemWorld
beats.source_passage: The tragic fact is that much of what made this area unique, lively, and . . . well, Harlem, during the fabled Jazz Era (aka the Harlem Renaissance), crumbled beneath the wrecking ball decades ago. What you now see—wide avenues, rows of brownstones, elegant apartment buildings—are somewhat an accident of history, the physical face of an area that housed a people but wasn't necessarily “of” that people (I'll explain below). Despite all this, Harlem remains the African-American capital of the United States (sometimes called the “capital for Africans throughout the world”), a one-of-a-kind area with much to recommend it. Architect Zevilla Jackson Preston best sums up its appeal in the book HarlemWorld, in which she writes, “Ultimately it is the energy on the street, the beat on the street—all of the beautiful Black people on the streets—that make the experience unique.”

beats.script_body: Harlem was settled in waves — Dutch farmers first, then their British counterparts, then poor Irish and Italian immigrants. But development only took off just before 1904, when the city's first subway line opened: a nine-and-a-half-mile snaking tunnel connecting Lower Manhattan with points as far north as 145th Street. In anticipation, an unprecedented housing boom hit the neighborhood, developers slapping up Victorian row house after row house for the crowds of upwardly mobile immigrants — middle-class Jews and Germans, primarily — they were certain would flood this newly commutable neighborhood. What they didn't anticipate were the recessions and panics of 1893, 1907, and 1910, which deflated the housing market and left them overbuilt.

9.5-mile tunnel to 145th St
Housing boom for middle-class Jews and Germans
Panics of 1893, 1907, 1910 deflated the market
beats.source_passage: Harlem was settled by a number of different groups over the years— Dutch farmers first, followed by their British counterparts, then poor Irish and Italian immigrants. But development only took off in the years just prior to 1904, when the city's first subway line opened, a 91⁄2-mile snaking tunnel connecting Lower Manhattan with points as far north as 145th Street. In anticipation of this event, an unprecedented housing boom hit the neighborhood, with developers slapping up Victorian row house after row house for the crowds of upwardly mobile immigrants—middle-class Jews and Germans, primarily—they were certain would soon flood this newly commutable neighborhood. What they didn't anticipate were recessions and panics in 1893, 1907, and 1910, which deflated the housing market and badly affected the development of large numbers of homes on the Upper West Side.

beats.script_body: Left with hundreds of unrentable homes, property owners began doing what nobody else had done in the history of the United States: renting or selling brand-new, beautifully appointed buildings to the race that had until then always made do with tumble-down ghetto housing no other group would accept. In 1905, pioneering real estate agent Philip Payton persuaded a white landlord to rent him 31 W. 133rd St. so he could re-lease it to African Americans — promising to pay a substantial $5 more per tenant per month, a lot of money in those days. Several other white landlords panicked and bought the building to evict the Black tenants, but by then it was too late: Payton had the funding to buy several other buildings, and Black migration into the area began in earnest.

beats.source_passage: Left with hundreds of unrentable homes, property owners soon began doing what nobody else had done in the history of the United States: renting or selling brand-new, often beautifully appointed buildings to the race that had, until that point, always made do with the tumble-down ghetto housing no other group would accept. In 1905, pioneering real estate agent Philip Payton persuaded a white landlord to rent him 31 W. 133rd St. so he could re-lease it to African Americans. The landlord accepted the offer because Payton promised to pay far more than the going rate, a substantial $5 more per tenant per month (a lot of money in those days). Several other white landlords panicked and bought the building in order to evict the Black tenants, but by then it was too late. Payton had the funding to buy several other buildings, and Black migration into the area began in earnest.

fact_check.notes: Year 1905 and 31 W 133rd St corroborated by web sources; Payton's vehicle was the Afro-American Realty Co. (not in source, not added).

beats.script_body: Look closely at the facade of this prominent Harlem church and you'll notice something you don't usually see on a church: several Stars of David. The building epitomizes the neighborhood's transformation. It was built in 1907 to be the neighborhood's first synagogue, and its architect — the first Jewish architect licensed in New York State — based the design on the Second Temple in Jerusalem, which had just been excavated and was making worldwide headlines. One prominent member of the congregation was Louis Blumstein, a name that returns later in this walk.

beats.script_body: In 1969, an act of kindness changed the lives of thousands of children. A young woman named Lorraine Hale was driving on 146th Street when she saw a drugged-out mother nodding off on the street, her two-month-old baby almost slipping from her arms. Ms. Hale got out, told the mother she needed treatment, and said she could leave the baby with her own mother — Clara McBride Hale — while she got sober. The next day the addicted mother did just that, and soon hundreds of babies were being left with 'Mother Hale,' who pioneered methods of treating babies born with addictions and also took in many HIV-positive babies.

beats.source_passage: We jump forward now a century to 1969 when an act of kindness changed the lives of thousands of children. A young woman named Lorraine Hale was driving on 146th Street when she saw a drugged-out mother nodding off on the street, her 2-month-old baby almost slipping from her arms. Ms. Hale got out of the car and told the mother she needed to get treatment and that she could leave the baby with her own mother—Clara McBride Hale—while she got sober. The next day the drug-addicted mother did just that, and soon hundreds of babies were being left with “Mother Hale,” who pioneered methods of treating babies born with addictions (and also took in a lot of HIV-positive babies).

beats.script_body: Mother Hale's work unfolded during the 1960s, '70s, and '80s — a period of steep decline for Harlem, when many landlords stopped maintaining and even abandoned their buildings. A 1960 census found only 50% of Harlem's housing sound, against 85% elsewhere in the city. As Harlem became synonymous with urban decay, Hale House — though a controversial institution later — was one of its few rays of hope. You can read more on the plaque at the door.

Harlem became synonymous with urban decay, and Hale House, though a controversial institution later, was one of its few rays of hope. You can read more about the house and its mission on the plaque at the door.

beats.script_body: This is not a famous building, but a very beautiful one — a good example of the talent enlisted to build Harlem's brownstones when the neighborhood was first developed. It's the work of architect William Tuthill, who later went on to design Carnegie Hall. As in many Gotham brownstones, the main entrance is on the second floor, not the ground floor. Why? It's a tradition left over from when the Dutch settled Manhattan: a people from a sea-level land prone to flooding, they placed their more important rooms above ground level and put the kitchen and servants' quarters below.

beats.trigger_address: east end of W. 122nd St at Mount Morris Park
beats.script_body: This park — long known as Mount Morris Park, named for General Roger Morris — was created in honor of the very first American victory in the Revolutionary War. It was near where you stand, on September 16, 1776, that George Washington engaged in what he called a 'brisk little skirmish' with the Redcoats. Just a month earlier the largest British expeditionary fleet in history had sailed into New York Harbor with 21,000 troops, a full 40% of all the men in the Royal Navy at the time. Those soldiers had slaughtered about 2,800 American militiamen at the Battle of Brooklyn, forcing Washington to flee Brooklyn by night to the northern reaches of Manhattan. Here, at the small battle called the Battle of Washington Heights, enemy buglers taunted the colonists by playing the call that traditionally ended a foxhunt. Enraged, Washington called for reinforcements and drove the Redcoats back to what is now the Upper West Side — the first time his soldiers had won an engagement, doing much to boost morale.

beats.source_passage: Named for General Roger Morris, this park was created in honor of the very first American victory in the Revolutionary War. It was in the vicinity of where you're standing now, on September 16, 1776, that George Washington engaged in what he called a “brisk little skirmish” with the Redcoats. Just 1 month earlier, the largest British expeditionary fleet in history had sailed into New York Harbor, bringing with it 21,000 troops, a full 40% of all the men serving in the Royal Navy at that time. In quick order, these trained soldiers slaughtered approximately 2,800 American militiamen at the Battle of Brooklyn, forcing Washington to escape Brooklyn under cover of night and hightail it to the northern reaches of Manhattan. At the small battle on this site, called the Battle of Washington Heights, enemy buglers taunted the colonists by playing the call that traditionally ended a foxhunt. Enraged, Washington called for reinforcements and drove the Redcoats back to what is now the Upper West Side. It was the first time his soldiers had won an engagement and did much to boost morale.

beats.script_body: Former President Bill Clinton set up his first post-presidency office on the top floor of this high-rise. He chose Harlem after a public outcry over the taxpayer-supported rent on his proposed Carnegie Hill office space — a whopping $850,000 a year. He's no longer headquartered here, but it was a fitting choice: Harlem is one of the Business Empowerment Zones his administration created, and the signs of the prosperity that policy engendered are all around you.

beats.script_body: Poet Langston Hughes bought this brownstone in 1947, likely with the royalties from writing the libretto to the Broadway musical Street Scene. His was an open house, with writers, musicians, and neighborhood friends dropping by at all hours. He was especially known for his kindness to local children: he called the garden in front 'The Children's Garden' and let the little ones plant whatever they wanted there. It was in this house that he wrote his famous book-length poem, Montage for a Dream Deferred.

beats.script_body: This pretty pocket park marks the site where the most famous hoarders of the pre-television age once lived: a pair of reclusive brothers who occupied their home here from the 1880s until their deaths in 1947. Rumors swirled about their compulsive behavior, but nobody knew the extent of it until both were found dead, surrounded by 140 tons of stuff — books, musical instruments, towering stacks of newspapers, baby carriages, guns, furniture, and all manner of junk, all rigged with booby traps to ward off outsiders. It took over a year to clear the house, which was eventually razed; it was rotting on its foundations.

beats.trigger_address: Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Blvd & 125th St
beats.script_body: This intersection is one of the most important in Harlem. Look first to the windswept northeast corner, where a statue of Adam Clayton Powell, Jr. — Harlem's first African-American congressman — stands. This is also the spot where Malcolm X spent many hours lecturing Harlem residents on behalf of the Nation of Islam. His message — 'We are Blacks first and everything else second' — was so powerful, and he such an effective orator, that before he left the NOI the organization had nearly half a million members; it dwindled rapidly after he resigned. His controversial message rejected non-violence and condemned integration as cultural suicide, going directly against the goals of the NAACP, the largest civil rights organization of the time.

beats.script_body: Across the street rises the tall white building with geometric patterns climbing its facade — the former Hotel Theresa. In 1960 a young Fidel Castro was scheduled to address the United Nations, but no hotel in town would take him and his contingent. After he threatened to camp on the U.N. lawn, the government ordered city hotels to accommodate him, but Castro quarreled with the midtown Shelburne Hotel he'd chosen. After a conversation with Malcolm X, he moved up here to the Theresa — a gesture of solidarity with Black Americans. Clashes between pro- and anti-Castro forces kept the 258 police officers guarding him busy, and on his second day Nikita Khrushchev came to visit; the combined police contingents created the greatest show of force Harlem had ever witnessed, unmatched to this day.

beats.source_passage: Now, look across the street at the tall white building with geometric patterns climbing up its facade, the former Hotel Theresa. If your olfactory glands have any imagination, you may detect a hint of Cuban cigar smoke in the air. In 1960, a young Fidel Castro was scheduled to speak at the United Nations, but no hotel in town would take him and his contingent. After he threatened to set up camp on the lawn of the United Nations, the government ordered city hotels to accommodate him, but Castro got into an argument with the midtown hotel he'd picked, the Shelburne Hotel. After a conversation with Malcolm X, he moved up here to the Hotel Theresa—a dramatic gesture Castro hoped would show his solidarity with Black Americans (and perhaps encourage a few to join the Communist Party). Repeated clashes between pro- and anti-Castro forces outside the hotel kept busy the 258 police officers assigned to guard him. On his second day at the Theresa, Nikita Khrushchev came to visit; his police contingent plus Castro's created the greatest show of force Harlem had ever witnessed (to this day, it hasn't been matched).

fact_check.notes: Castro's 1960 stay at Hotel Theresa during the UN visit, the Shelburne dispute, and the Khrushchev visit are corroborated by web sources.

beats.script_body: When it opened in 1900, Blumstein's was the neighborhood's largest and most exclusive store, built at a cost of $1 million — note the beautifully worked copper ornamentation on the facade, a mix of Art Deco and Spanish Renaissance. It was owned by Louis Blumstein, the synagogue congregant from the tour's start. Although the vast majority of its clientele was African American, Blumstein's refused to hire any Black clerks — a maddening policy during the Great Depression. In 1934 the Urban League, spearheaded by Reverends John H. Johnson and Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., launched a boycott and picket of the store. beats.source_passage: When it opened its doors in 1900, this was the neighborhood's largest and most exclusive store, built at a cost of $1 million (notice the beautifully worked copper ornamentation on the facade, a mix of Art Deco and Spanish Renaissance in its patterning). And yes, it was owned by Louis Blumstein, whom we discussed at the beginning of this tour. Although the vast majority of its clientele was African American, Blumstein's refused to hire any Black store clerks (a particularly maddening policy in the Great Depression, when jobs were scarce). In 1934, the Urban League began a campaign, spearheaded by Reverends John H. Johnson and Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., to boycott and picket the store until it changed its hiring practices. The action lasted 2 months, with picketers carrying signs with the simple but effective request don't buy where you can't work. Blumstein's finally relented, hiring 34 African-American women as clerks. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. often spoke of this strike in his speeches as an example of the power of non-violent protest.

fact_check.notes: 1934 'Don't Buy Where You Can't Work' Blumstein's boycott corroborated. beats.script_body: In 1958, Dr. King himself was at the center of history at Blumstein's. He was seated at a table signing copies of his book Strides Towards Freedom when a Black woman named Izola Ware Curry reached the front of the line. After asking, 'Are you Martin Luther King?' she pulled a letter opener from the book she was carrying and, shouting 'You Communist, you Communist!', stabbed him in the chest. King was rushed to Harlem Hospital with the blade still in — had it been removed, he would have bled to death — and underwent surgery. The next morning the New York Times reported that had King sneezed, he would have died, as the blade was touching his aorta. From his hospital bed, King issued a letter of forgiveness to Curry, who was committed to an asylum; she had a long history of mental instability.

beats.script_body: For years, 125th Street was known as the 'Great Black Way,' a play on Broadway's 'Great White Way' — this was the theater district of Harlem. Only a few of those great show palaces still exist, but right in front of you is the most famous and influential: the Apollo Theater. A whites-only burlesque house until 1934, it changed its policy and its lineup that year, becoming a music hall in January and introducing the legendary 'Amateur Night' a few months later.
